title: Predicate Logic and Quantifiers
subtitle: Opening up the atoms: the logic of 'all', 'some' and 'everyone loves someone'
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what predicates, names, variables and the two quantifiers (∀ and ∃) are.

By the end you will be able to translate the four classic forms ('All F are G', 'Some F are G', 'No F are G', 'Some F are not G') into predicate logic and avoid the two most common translation mistakes.
By the end you will be able to explain quantifier scope and spot the quantifier-shift fallacy.
By the end you will be able to say why Frege's logic replaced Aristotle's syllogistic as the standard logic of philosophy and mathematics.
By the end you will be able to describe one key limitation of predicate logic: that there is no truth-table-style test that always decides validity.
hook:
Consider two sentences. "Everybody loves somebody." "Somebody is loved by everybody." They use the same words and seem to say nearly the same thing. They do not. The first is probably true: each person has someone they love, perhaps a different someone for each. The second claims there is one single person whom literally everyone loves, which is almost certainly false. A logic that cannot tell these apart is not fit for serious reasoning.

In Lesson 1 you learned propositional logic, which treats "Socrates is mortal" as an unbreakable atom P. That logic is blind to the words *all*, *some* and *every* that do so much work in arguments. Today we open up the atoms. The tool we use, **predicate logic** (also called first-order logic), was introduced by Gottlob Frege in 1879, and you met its revolutionary arrival on Day 69. Now you get to use it.

sections.heading: Names, Predicates and Variables
sections.body:
Predicate logic breaks a simple sentence into two kinds of pieces. A **name** (logicians say an *individual constant*) picks out one particular thing: lowercase letters like s for Socrates or p for Paris. A **predicate** says something about things: uppercase letters like H for "is human" or M for "is mortal." We write the predicate first and the name after it, so "Socrates is human" becomes Hs and "Socrates is mortal" becomes Ms.

Some predicates relate two or more things. Let L stand for "loves." Then Lab means "a loves b," and Lba means "b loves a," which is a different claim, as many sad songs attest. These are called **relations** or many-place predicates. "Paris is between Rouen and Lyon" needs a three-place predicate: Bprl.

Next come **variables**: x, y, z. A variable is like a pronoun, a placeholder that does not name anything in particular. "x is human" (Hx) is not yet true or false, any more than "it is human" is, until we know what "it" refers to. Hx is called an **open formula**.

To turn an open formula into a full claim, we can either replace the variable with a name, or bind it with a quantifier. All the propositional connectives from Lesson 1 carry over unchanged: ¬, ∧, ∨, → and ↔. So (Hs ∧ Ms) means "Socrates is human and Socrates is mortal."

One more ingredient: a **domain**, the collection of things our variables range over. If the domain is "all people," then "everything" means "everyone." Stating the domain prevents a lot of confusion: "Everyone passed" is true of my class, not of the human race.

sections.heading: The Two Quantifiers and the Classic Translations
sections.body:
A **quantifier** tells us how many things in the domain satisfy a formula. Predicate logic needs only two.

- The **universal quantifier**, ∀x, read "for every x" or "for all x." ∀x Mx says "Everything is mortal."
- The **existential quantifier**, ∃x, read "there is at least one x such that." ∃x Hx says "Something is human."

Note that "some" in logic means *at least one*, possibly all. "Some students passed" is true even if every student passed, although in conversation it might suggest otherwise.

Now the four classic forms Aristotle studied (Day 17), with domain "everything":
- All F are G: ∀x(Fx → Gx). "For anything, if it is an F, it is a G."
- Some F are G: ∃x(Fx ∧ Gx). "There is something that is both F and G."
- No F are G: ∀x(Fx → ¬Gx), or equivalently ¬∃x(Fx ∧ Gx).
- Some F are not G: ∃x(Fx ∧ ¬Gx).

Two mistakes are so common that every logic teacher warns against them.

**Mistake 1**: translating "All humans are mortal" as ∀x(Hx ∧ Mx). That says "Everything is both human and mortal," which makes every rock and galaxy a human. Universal claims need the conditional: the claim is only about things that are human.

**Mistake 2**: translating "Some humans are mortal" as ∃x(Hx → Mx). Recall from Lesson 1 that a conditional with a false antecedent is true. So any single non-human thing, like a pebble, makes Hx → Mx true, and the formula would be true even in a world with no humans at all. Existential claims need the conjunction.

The rule of thumb: **∀ goes with →, ∃ goes with ∧.**

The quantifiers are linked by negation, just as De Morgan's laws link ∧ and ∨:
- ¬∀x Fx is equivalent to ∃x ¬Fx. "Not everything is F" means "Something is not F."
- ¬∃x Fx is equivalent to ∀x ¬Fx. "Nothing is F" means "Everything is not F."

This is why one counterexample refutes a universal generalization: to deny "All swans are white" you need only one non-white swan.

sections.heading: Scope: Why Word Order Matters
sections.body:
Return to the hook. With domain "people" and Lxy meaning "x loves y":
- "Everybody loves somebody": ∀x∃y Lxy. For each person x, there is some y (which may differ from person to person) whom x loves.
- "Somebody is loved by everybody": ∃y∀x Lxy. There is a single y such that every x loves that y.

The only difference is the order of the quantifiers. The **scope** of a quantifier is the part of the formula it governs, and when one quantifier sits inside the scope of another, the inner one may depend on the outer. In ∀x∃y, the choice of y can vary with x. In ∃y∀x, y is fixed first, and then must work for everyone.

The second formula implies the first (if one person is loved by all, then everybody loves somebody: that person). But the first does not imply the second. Moving from ∀x∃y to ∃y∀x is a classic error called the **quantifier-shift fallacy**. Compare: "Every child has a mother, so there is some woman who is every child's mother."

Philosophers have accused famous arguments of this slip. The opening of Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* (Day 20) moves from the claim that every action aims at some good to the idea that there is a good at which all things aim. Some commentators read this as a quantifier shift; others argue Aristotle never intended the inference that way. Similarly, critics of some cosmological arguments (Day 35) ask whether "Every event has a cause" really gets you to "There is one cause of every event." Whatever the verdict on these historical cases, predicate logic makes the question precise.

Scope also explains ambiguous English. "All that glitters is not gold" literally says ∀x(Gx → ¬Ox): nothing that glitters is gold, which is false (gold glitters). What the proverb means is ¬∀x(Gx → Ox): not everything that glitters is gold. The negation should take wide scope over the quantifier, but English grammar puts it in the middle. Similarly, "Everyone didn't come" can mean nobody came or not everyone came. Formal logic forces you to choose.

sections.heading: Why Frege's Logic Beat Aristotle's
sections.body:
Aristotle's syllogistic reigned for over two thousand years; Kant (Day 55) even remarked that logic had not needed to take a single step forward since Aristotle. Frege's *Begriffsschrift* ("Concept-Script," 1879) ended that reign. Why?

**First, relations and multiple generality.** Syllogistic handles sentences with one subject term and one predicate term, like "All S are P." It struggles with relations and with sentences containing more than one quantifier. In the nineteenth century Augustus De Morgan pointed out a simple valid inference that syllogistic could not capture: since a horse is an animal, the head of a horse is the head of an animal. In predicate logic this becomes provable: if ∀x(Hx → Ax), then anything that is the head of some horse is the head of some animal. Mathematics is full of such multiple generality. "For every number there is a larger number" is ∀x∃y(y > x), and the definition of a limit in calculus stacks three quantifiers: for every ε there is a δ such that for all x ... Syllogistic simply cannot express these, which is why Frege, who wanted to show that arithmetic rests on logic, needed something new.

**Second, unification.** Frege's system contains both propositional logic (Lesson 1) and syllogistic as fragments. Every valid syllogism can be checked in predicate logic. The old logic was not wrong; it was a small part of a larger whole.

**Third, existential import.** Traditional logic assumed that "All S are P" implies "Some S are P," which goes wrong when there are no S. On the modern reading, "All unicorns have one horn," ∀x(Ux → Ox), is (vacuously) true because there are no unicorns, while "Some unicorns have one horn" is false. Many traditional relations in the so-called square of opposition fail without the existence assumption. Modern logic makes such assumptions explicit premises rather than hidden ones.

**Fourth, identity and counting.** Adding an identity sign (=) lets us express number. "There are at least two moons" is ∃x∃y(Mx ∧ My ∧ ¬x = y). Russell's theory of descriptions (Day 69) uses exactly this machinery: "The present King of France is bald" becomes "There is exactly one present King of France, and he is bald": ∃x(Kx ∧ ∀y(Ky → y = x) ∧ Bx). Since nothing is the present King of France, the sentence is simply false, and the puzzle about talking of non-existent things dissolves.

One caution against a triumphalist story: medieval logicians, such as William of Ockham (Day 36) and Jean Buridan, developed sophisticated theories of quantification and scope well beyond Aristotle, and historians now give them more credit than early twentieth-century logicians did.

sections.heading: Translating English: A Workshop
sections.body:
Translation is a skill, and the best way to learn it is through worked examples. Domain: people. Let S = is a student, P = passed, T = is a teacher, Axy = x admires y, and a = Ada.

1. "Every student passed." ∀x(Sx → Px).
2. "Not every student passed." ¬∀x(Sx → Px), equivalently ∃x(Sx ∧ ¬Px): some student did not pass.
3. "Only students passed." Careful! "Only" reverses the direction: if someone passed, they are a student. ∀x(Px → Sx). "Only members may enter" does not say all members may enter.
4. "Ada admires every teacher." ∀x(Tx → Aax).
5. "Some student admires every teacher." ∃x(Sx ∧ ∀y(Ty → Axy)).
6. "Every student admires some teacher." ∀x(Sx → ∃y(Ty ∧ Axy)). Compare with 5: a scope difference again.
7. "No one admires a teacher who failed them." English is ambiguous about what "a" means here; it is best read universally: ∀x∀y((Ty ∧ Fyx) → ¬Axy), where Fyx means y failed x.

The little word "any" is tricky. "If anyone cheats, they will be expelled" is universal: ∀x(Cx → Ex). But "If anyone cheats, the exam is void" means if there is at least one cheater: ∃x Cx → V. Both use "any," but the logical form differs because of what the pronoun refers back to.

Translation is not merely mechanical. It requires interpreting what a speaker means, and sometimes the honest answer is that a sentence is ambiguous and has two translations. That is a feature, not a bug. Many philosophical disputes begin when someone realizes that a premise everyone accepted had two readings: one true, one that the argument needs.

sections.heading: Validity, Models and a Surprising Limit
sections.body:
How do we test validity in predicate logic? Truth tables no longer work, because the domain might contain infinitely many things. Instead we use **interpretations** (also called models): a choice of domain plus a meaning for each predicate and name. An argument is valid if every interpretation that makes the premises true makes the conclusion true. To show an argument invalid, you build a countermodel.

Example: "Some philosophers are Greek. Some Greeks are poets. So some philosophers are poets." Invalid. Countermodel: domain = {1, 2}; philosopher = {1}; Greek = {1, 2}; poet = {2}. Both premises are true and the conclusion false. Small countermodels like this are the predicate logician's counterexample rows.

Two great results then define the subject. In 1929–30 Kurt Gödel proved the **completeness** of first-order logic: every valid argument can be proven with a standard set of rules. So proof and validity line up perfectly, as they did in propositional logic.

But in 1936 Alonzo Church and Alan Turing independently proved that first-order logic is **undecidable**: there is no mechanical procedure that, given any argument, always halts and correctly answers "valid" or "invalid." If an argument is valid, a systematic search will eventually find a proof; but if it is invalid, the search may run forever without telling you. The dream associated with Leibniz (Day 46), of settling every dispute by calculation, is impossible even for pure logic. Turing's proof of this result introduced the abstract machines that became the theory of the modern computer. Lesson 5 will meet Gödel again, with a more famous and more unsettling theorem.

modernConnection.title: Every Database Query Is a Quantified Sentence
modernConnection.body:
In 1970 the IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd published a paper proposing the relational model of data, which became the basis for almost every business database on earth. Codd's insight was that a database is essentially an interpretation in the sense of this lesson: a domain of objects (customers, orders, products) plus relations among them (who ordered what). Querying the database is asking which objects satisfy a formula of predicate logic. Codd explicitly built his query language on first-order logic, and the language SQL that descends from his work still bears the marks.

Suppose you want "customers who have ordered every product in the sale category." That is ∀y(Sy → Oxy): a universal quantifier nested inside a query. SQL has no direct "for all," so programmers write it the way the negation rules in this lesson suggest: find customers for whom there does NOT EXIST a sale product that they have NOT ordered. Database programmers who have never heard of Frege apply ¬∃¬ every day.

Scope mistakes are a real source of bugs. Confuse "customers who bought some product from every category" with "customers who bought every product from some category" and you will send a marketing email to the wrong million people. The same issues matter in law. A contract saying "The tenant may not keep a dog or a cat" and a regulation requiring "approval of any change" invite the scope and "any" ambiguities we studied, and courts spend real time resolving them.

The connection has limits. Real databases make a "closed world assumption" (if an order is not recorded, it did not happen), which classical logic does not make, and SQL uses a three-valued logic with NULL for unknown values, which can produce results that surprise anyone trained on two truth values. And the large language models now used to answer questions in plain English do not translate into formal logic first; they can handle ambiguity gracefully but can also make quantifier-shift errors that a formal system never would. That is one reason some AI researchers advocate combining language models with logical reasoning tools.

vocabulary.definition: An expression that says something about one or more things, written as a capital letter (e.g. Hx: x is human).
vocabulary.example: In 'Socrates is wise', 'is wise' is the predicate, written W, so the sentence becomes Ws.

vocabulary.definition: The symbol meaning 'for every x' or 'for all x' in the domain.
vocabulary.example: ∀x(Rx → Ox), 'every raven is black', is refuted by a single non-black raven.

vocabulary.definition: The symbol meaning 'there is at least one x such that'.
vocabulary.example: ∃x(Sx ∧ Bx) says that at least one swan is black.

vocabulary.definition: The collection of things the variables range over in a given context.
vocabulary.example: With the domain set to 'people in this room', 'everyone is seated' can be true.

vocabulary.definition: The part of a formula that a quantifier or negation governs; changing the order of quantifiers changes the meaning.
vocabulary.example: ∀x∃y Lxy and ∃y∀x Lxy differ only in scope, yet one says much more than the other.

vocabulary.definition: The invalid inference from 'for every x there is some y' to 'there is some y for every x'.
vocabulary.example: 'Every road leads somewhere, so there is a place every road leads' commits a quantifier shift.

vocabulary.definition: The assumption that a universal statement 'All S are P' implies that some S exist.
vocabulary.example: Modern logic drops existential import, so 'All trespassers will be prosecuted' is true even if there are no trespassers.

vocabulary.definition: The property of a logic for which no mechanical procedure always correctly determines validity in finite time.
vocabulary.example: Because first-order logic is undecidable, no computer program can check every possible argument for validity.

thinkingExercise.title: Find the Hidden Quantifiers
thinkingExercise.prompt: Ordinary arguments hide their quantifiers. Your task is to dig them out of real sentences and see whether the reasoning survives.
steps: Collect three sentences from news headlines, adverts or your own conversations that contain words like 'all', 'every', 'some', 'no', 'only' or 'any'.
Choose a domain and predicate letters for each, and translate each sentence into predicate logic. If a sentence is ambiguous, give both translations.
For one sentence, write its negation in English and in symbols, using the rules ¬∀ = ∃¬ and ¬∃ = ∀¬. Check that your English negation really is the contradiction of the original.
Find or invent one argument that commits the quantifier-shift fallacy, and describe a small countermodel (domain and predicates) showing it is invalid.

summary: Predicate logic splits sentences into names, predicates (including relations) and variables, and binds variables with the quantifiers ∀ ('for all') and ∃ ('there is at least one').
Universal claims pair with the conditional, ∀x(Fx → Gx), and existential claims pair with conjunction, ∃x(Fx ∧ Gx); mixing them up is the commonest translation mistake.
Quantifier order and scope change meaning: 'everybody loves somebody' does not imply 'somebody is loved by everybody', and inferring otherwise is the quantifier-shift fallacy.
Frege's logic replaced Aristotle's because it handles relations, multiple quantifiers and identity, contains syllogistic as a fragment, and makes existential assumptions explicit.
First-order logic is complete (Gödel, 1929–30) but undecidable (Church and Turing, 1936): every validity can be proved, but no mechanical test settles every case.

quiz.question: Which is the correct translation of 'All dogs are loyal' (D = is a dog, L = is loyal)?
quiz.explanation: Universal statements use the conditional: for anything, if it is a dog, it is loyal. ∀x(Dx ∧ Lx) would make everything a dog, and ∀x(Lx → Dx) says only dogs are loyal.

quiz.question: Why is ∃x(Dx → Lx) a bad translation of 'Some dogs are loyal'?
options: It is true as soon as there is any non-dog, even if no dog is loyal
It says every dog is loyal
It cannot be true if there are loyal dogs
quiz.explanation: A conditional with a false antecedent is true, so any non-dog makes Dx → Lx true. The correct form is ∃x(Dx ∧ Lx).

quiz.question: ∃y∀x Lxy ('someone is loved by everyone') logically implies ∀x∃y Lxy ('everyone loves someone').
quiz.explanation: If one particular person is loved by all, then everyone loves at least that person. The converse inference is the invalid one.

quiz.question: 'Every patient has a doctor, so there is a doctor who treats every patient.' What is wrong with this inference?
quiz.explanation: It moves from ∀x∃y to ∃y∀x, illegitimately fixing one doctor for all patients.

quiz.question: 'Only registered voters may vote' is best translated (R = registered, V = may vote) as:
quiz.explanation: 'Only' reverses the direction: if you may vote, you are registered. It does not say that every registered person may vote.

quiz.question: On the modern reading, 'All unicorns have one horn' is true because there are no unicorns.
quiz.explanation: ∀x(Ux → Ox) is vacuously true when nothing satisfies Ux, since every instance has a false antecedent. Modern logic drops Aristotle's existential import.

quiz.question: Which of the following best explains why Frege needed a new logic to found mathematics?
options: Syllogistic could not handle relations and statements with several nested quantifiers
quiz.explanation: Mathematical claims like 'for every number there is a larger one' involve relations and multiple generality, which syllogistic cannot express. Aristotle's valid syllogisms remain valid.

quiz.question: What did Church and Turing prove in 1936 about first-order logic?
options: No mechanical procedure can decide the validity of every argument
Every valid argument can be checked by a truth table
quiz.explanation: First-order logic is undecidable. It is nonetheless complete (Gödel), so every valid argument has a proof, but invalid arguments may never be recognized as such by a search.

quiz.question: 'Not all students passed' is logically equivalent to 'No students passed'.
quiz.explanation: ¬∀x(Sx → Px) is equivalent to ∃x(Sx ∧ ¬Px): at least one student failed. 'No students passed' is much stronger.

goDeeper.body:
Why is it called *first-order* logic? Because its quantifiers range only over individual objects. **Second-order logic** also lets you quantify over properties: "There is a property that Socrates and Plato share" becomes ∃F(Fs ∧ Fp). This is more expressive. In second-order logic you can pin down the natural numbers uniquely and express Leibniz's identity of indiscernibles (Day 46) as a single formula: ∀x∀y(∀F(Fx ↔ Fy) → x = y). But second-order logic (with its standard semantics) is not complete: no proof system captures all its validities. Quine (Day 74) famously dismissed it as "set theory in sheep's clothing," arguing that quantifying over properties smuggles in mathematical objects. Others, like George Boolos, defended it by reading second-order quantifiers as plural expressions ("there are some things such that ...").

A related debate concerns what quantifiers commit us to. Quine's slogan "to be is to be the value of a variable" means that the things your best theory quantifies over are the things you believe exist. If your physics says ∃x(x is an electron), you are committed to electrons; if your mathematics says ∃x(x is a prime greater than 100), are you committed to numbers? This makes predicate logic a tool for ontology, the study of what exists (Day 18). Meanwhile, the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem shows that a first-order theory with an infinite model has models of different infinite sizes, including countable ones, a strange result (Skolem's paradox) that suggests first-order logic cannot fully fix what our theories are about.

readings.author: W. V. O. Quine
readings.note: A classic textbook by a great philosopher-logician, with careful discussion of translating English into logic.

questions: Does the existential quantifier capture everything we mean by 'exists'? Think about 'Sherlock Holmes doesn't exist' or 'There are numbers between 2 and 3'.
Undecidability shows that some questions in logic cannot be settled by mechanical calculation. Does that tell us anything about whether human reasoning is more than computation?
